# Voice and tone

How the product speaks: the words in every component.

## The five answers

| Question | Answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which kinds of copy does it need? | Labels, messages and headlines | Headlines carry the campaign. |
| How many tones does it use? | One per moment | Playful in headlines, plain in errors. |
| How is the voice defined? | Principles and examples | Principles and examples guide each campaign's writers. |
| How does it sound? | Playful | Big words, few of them. |
| Where do the words matter most? | Headlines and buttons | Words work hardest in headlines and buttons. |

## When to use what

| Situation | Use | Not | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A button label | A short verb that moves: Join, Try, Go | "Learn more" | Big moments need verbs with energy. Example: “Join the drop” |
| The words of an error | Plain first, a light touch after | A joke before the fix | Playful copy must never hide what went wrong. Example: “That email doesn't look right. Check it and try again.” |
| A success message | Celebrate, briefly | A long thank-you | A short celebration is remembered. Example: “You're on the list. See you at launch.” |
| An empty state | Playful, with a clear next step | A dead end | Playful words still need a way forward. Example: “Nothing here yet. Go find something you love.” |
| A confirmation question | Plain. No jokes when something is lost. | Playful copy | Loss is never the moment for a joke. Example: “Remove this from your list? You can add it back later.” |
| A first visit | One bold line and one button | A paragraph of copy | Visitors from a social post give a few seconds. Example: “The drop is coming. Be first.” |
